ANSWER — 14 CFR § 91.151(a), fuel beyond the first point of intended landing, airplane, VFR, at normal cruising speed:

  • DAY:   30 minutes
  • NIGHT: 45 minutes

Both are minimums expressed as time at normal cruising speed, and both are fuel that must remain AFTER flying to the first point of intended landing.

1. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, 14 CFR § 91.151, current as of the 2026-01-01 CFR revision; identical in eCFR and GovInfo):

"§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.
(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed—
(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or
(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes.
(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

2. HOW THE REQUIREMENT IS COMPUTED (so the figures are applied correctly):

Required fuel at brake release =
  (fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing, considering wind and forecast weather)
  + (fuel for the reserve time at normal cruising speed)
where reserve time = 30 min (day) or 45 min (night), for an airplane.

In time terms: usable endurance at normal cruising speed must be at least [time to first point of intended landing + 0:30] by day, or [+ 0:45] by night. Worked example: a 2:10 estimated leg to the first point of intended landing requires at least 2:40 of endurance by day and 2:55 by night, at normal cruising speed, considering forecast wind.

3. POINTS THAT ARE PART OF THE RULE, NOT COMMENTARY:

  • Measured after the first point of intended landing. The reserve is not available for the leg to that point; it is additive to it.
  • "Assuming normal cruising speed." The reserve is a time, not a distance and not a fixed gallon figure; convert at the airplane's normal cruising speed (and normal cruise fuel flow) to get the fuel quantity to actually load. Example: 120 KTAS normal cruise ⇒ 30 min = 60 NM equivalent / 45 min = 90 NM equivalent, then converted to gallons/lb at cruise fuel flow.
  • "Considering wind and forecast weather conditions." Wind and forecast must be accounted for in the fuel-to-the-first-point portion; they do not reduce the 30/45-minute reserve times.
  • It is a pre-flight prohibition: "No person may begin a flight ... unless." Compliance is judged at dispatch, on the fuel aboard at engine start, not adjusted en route.
  • Airplanes only in (a). Rotorcraft are governed by § 91.151(b): 20 minutes, day or night, no day/night split. Do not apply the 30/45 figures to a helicopter.
  • No alternate-airport fuel requirement under VFR. Unlike IFR (§ 91.167(a)(2)), § 91.151 requires no fuel to a destination alternate. Caution: § 91.167(a)(3) also uses "45 minutes," but that is the IFR post-alternate reserve; it is a coincidence of numbers and is NOT the source of the night VFR figure. Night VFR 45 minutes comes from § 91.151(a)(2) alone.
  • "Night" for § 91.151(a)(2) is the § 1.1 definition: "Night means the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac, converted to local time." A flight that will be in the air during any part of that period should be planned to the 45-minute figure; if the flight is wholly in the day period, 30 minutes applies.
  • This is a regulatory floor, not a flight-planning target. Standard practice (and any operator's OpSpec/GOM) may impose higher reserves; the higher number governs. Conversely, no operator minimum can go below 30/45.

4. SELF-CHECK OF THE STATED VALUES:

  • Day = 30 minutes: matches § 91.151(a)(1) exactly; no other figure in this deliverable is lower than it for airplanes.
  • Night = 45 minutes: matches § 91.151(a)(2) exactly; it exceeds the day figure, consistent with the regulation's ordering, and nothing in this deliverable sets a threshold below it for night airplanes.
  • Rotorcraft 20 minutes is quoted only under § 91.151(b) and is never applied to the airplane answer.
  • IFR 45 minutes (§ 91.167) is identified as an IFR rule and explicitly disclaimed as the basis for the night VFR value.
  • No computed or example figure in this deliverable contradicts a limit stated elsewhere in it (worked example 2:40 day / 2:55 night = leg + 0:30 / leg + 0:45, consistent with the stated reserves).

HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS FOR PROPERTY-CARRYING CMVs — 49 CFR § 395.3(a)

SCOPE. Driver of a property-carrying commercial motor vehicle in interstate commerce, fully subject to Part 395, with no exemption or exception under § 395.1 in play. Current text of the regulation as printed in the 2025 edition of the CFR (49 CFR vol. 5, revised as of Oct. 1, 2025) and as published on eCFR; source history 76 FR 81188 (Dec. 27, 2011), as amended at 78 FR 58485, 78 FR 64181, 84 FR 48081, and 85 FR 33452 (June 1, 2020). The three figures below are unchanged across all four sources checked (eCFR current, GovInfo 2025 HTML, GovInfo 2025 PDF, GovInfo 2023 XML).

=== ANSWERS ===

1. CONSECUTIVE OFF-DUTY HOURS REQUIRED BEFORE DRIVING: 10 hours.
   Authority: § 395.3(a)(1) — 'Start of work shift. A driver may not drive without first taking 10 consecutive hours off duty.'

2. CONSECUTIVE ON-DUTY HOURS AFTER WHICH DRIVING IS PROHIBITED: 14 hours.
   Authority: § 395.3(a)(2) — '14-hour period. A driver may not drive after a period of 14 consecutive hours after coming on-duty following 10 consecutive hours off-duty.'
   Precision note (material — read this before applying the number): the trigger is not 14 accumulated hours of on-duty time. It is the lapse of 14 consecutive clock hours beginning at the moment the driver comes on duty after the 10-hour break. Off-duty, sleeper-berth, or on-duty-not-driving time taken inside that 14-hour span does not pause, extend, or toll the clock. A driver who comes on duty at 06:00 and takes three hours off duty at midday may still not drive after 20:00 that day. Only a qualifying interruption that resets the calculation (a new 10-consecutive-hour off-duty period, the split provision in § 395.1(g), or the 34-hour restart in § 395.3(c)) restarts the 14-hour window.

3. TOTAL DRIVING HOURS PERMITTED WITHIN THAT PERIOD: 11 hours.
   Authority: § 395.3(a)(3)(i) — 'Driving time. A driver may drive a total of 11 hours during the period specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section.'
   The 11 hours are a cap on driving time inside the 14-hour window, not a separate 11-hour day and not 11 hours per 24-hour calendar day. It is the total for that window; the window (and the 11 hours) is available again only after the driver satisfies § 395.3(a)(1) with 10 consecutive hours off duty.

=== HOW THE THREE NUMBERS INTERLOCK ===

- The 11-hour driving cap is subordinate to the 14-hour window: whatever driving the driver does must be completed within the 14 consecutive hours that began at coming on duty. Driving 11 hours does not create an entitlement to be driving at hour 13 of the window if the driving is already exhausted; conversely, reaching hour 14 with driving time remaining ends driving anyway.
- The 8-hour/30-minute interruption rule, § 395.3(a)(3)(ii): except for drivers qualifying under the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e)(1) or (2), driving is not permitted if more than 8 hours of driving time have passed without at least one consecutive 30-minute interruption in driving status. The interruption may be satisfied by off-duty, sleeper berth, or on-duty-not-driving time, or any combination of them. This rule does NOT reduce the 11-hour total: a driver may run 8 hours of driving, take a 30-minute interruption, and then drive the remaining 3 hours, all inside the 14-hour window (8 + 0.5 + 3 = 11.5 elapsed hours, which fits within 14).
- Worked example. Driver comes on duty 06:00 after 10 consecutive hours off duty. The 14-hour window closes at 20:00; no driving is permitted at or after that point. Within 06:00–20:00 the driver may accumulate at most 11 hours of driving, and must take a consecutive 30-minute interruption no later than the point at which 8 cumulative hours of driving have elapsed. Non-driving on-duty work (loading, fueling, paperwork) consumes the 14-hour window but not the 11-hour driving allowance.

=== WHAT THESE THREE FIGURES DO NOT COVER (state explicitly to the requester) ===

- § 395.3(a)(3)(ii) — the 8-hour/30-minute interruption requirement, described above; it can make an 11-hour driving day unlawful in practice if the interruption is not taken.
- § 395.3(b) — the 60-hour/7-consecutive-day limit (carrier not operating every day of the week) and the 70-hour/8-consecutive-day limit (carrier operating every day of the week). These are cumulative on-duty limits that sit on top of the (a) limits; a driver can be fully compliant with the 10/14/11 figures and still be prohibited from driving by (b).
- § 395.3(c) — the 34-hour restart, which permits a 7- or 8-day period to end with the beginning of an off-duty period of 34 or more consecutive hours.
- § 395.1 exceptions and exemptions, which the opening clause of § 395.3(a) ('Except as otherwise provided in § 395.1') expressly preserves. The ones most likely to change the answer for a given driver are the short-haul exceptions in § 395.1(e), adverse driving conditions in § 395.1(b), the Alaska property-carrying rules in § 395.1(h)(1) (15 hours driving / 20 hours on duty following 10 consecutive hours off duty), the oilfield exemption in § 395.1(d), and the split sleeper-berth provision in § 395.1(g).
- Caution: the split sleeper-berth mechanics in § 395.1(g) and the adverse-driving extension in § 395.1(b) were not part of the source text retrieved for this analysis, so no specific split composition or extension figure is asserted here. If the driver relies on either provision, pull the current § 395.1(g) or § 395.1(b) text before applying these numbers; the 10/14/11 figures above are the baseline that applies absent a qualifying § 395.1 provision.
- Passenger-carrying vehicles are governed by § 395.5, not § 395.3 (10 hours driving / 15 hours on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty). Do not apply the figures above to passenger operations.

=== CITATIONS ===

49 CFR § 395.3(a)(1), (a)(2), (a)(3)(i); § 395.3(a)(3)(ii); § 395.3(b); § 395.3(c). Source text: eCFR, 49 CFR subtitle B, chapter III, subchapter B, part 395, subpart A, § 395.3 (fetched 2026-11-23); GovInfo, CFR 2025 title 49 vol. 5, § 395.3 (HTML and PDF, revised as of Oct. 1, 2025).

The first reads: "(i) More than 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off-duty;"

45 CFR § 164.404(b) — TIMELINESS OF INDIVIDUAL BREACH NOTIFICATION

=====================================================================
I. OPERATIVE ANSWER
=====================================================================

Ask 1 — By when must a covered entity notify an individual?
A covered entity must notify each affected individual 'without unreasonable delay' and 'in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.' § 164.404(b).

These are two separate obligations, not one. 'Without unreasonable delay' is an independent, affirmative duty: notification must go out as soon as reasonably practicable under the circumstances of the investigation, and the 60-day figure is a ceiling, not a safe harbor. A notice sent on day 45 after an investigation that reasonably required 10 days still violates § 164.404(b). Conversely, a notice sent on day 5 satisfies the outer limit but could still violate the 'without unreasonable delay' prong if the entity sat on a completed investigation.

Ask 2 — Outer limit: 60 calendar days.
'Calendar days,' not business days. Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays count toward the 60. There is no extension if day 60 falls on a weekend or holiday, and no extension for a pending forensic investigation, a pending law-enforcement request (absent § 164.412), or internal approval cycles.

Ask 3 — From what event does the limit run?
From 'discovery of a breach' — not from the date of the breach itself, not from the date the incident was confirmed by outside counsel or a forensic vendor, and not from the date the affected population was finally enumerated.

'Discovery' is defined by § 164.404(a)(2): the breach is treated as discovered 'as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity.' Knowledge is imputed: the covered entity 'shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency).'

=====================================================================
II. CONTROLLING TEXT
=====================================================================

§ 164.404(a)(1) — General rule:
'A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected health information, notify each individual whose unsecured protected health information has been, or is reasonably believed by the covered entity to have been, accessed, acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of such breach.'

§ 164.404(a)(2) — Breaches treated as discovered:
'For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§ 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of agency).'

§ 164.404(b) — Timeliness of notification:
'Except as provided in § 164.412, a covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.'

(Source: eCFR, 45 CFR § 164.404, fetched 2026-11-23T12:23:08Z, sha256 c22a00386c9d; cross-checked against GovInfo CFR-2025-title45-vol2, sha256 d8b81574bb0b. Wording identical in both.)

=====================================================================
III. ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT ANALYSIS
=====================================================================

A. 'Without unreasonable delay'
- Functional test: how long did a reasonable, diligent covered entity need, given the scope and complexity of the incident, to determine (i) that a breach occurred, (ii) the identity and contact information of affected individuals, and (iii) the content elements required by § 164.404(c)?
- Delay attributable to the entity's own choices — queue backlog, vendor contract disputes, awaiting a final polished report, marketing/PR review — is generally unreasonable delay.
- Delay attributable to genuine necessity — a forensic scope determination needed to identify who was affected, or a law-enforcement instruction under § 164.412 — is not, but the entity bears the burden of documenting why.
- Practical rule: begin drafting and staging the notice on the day of discovery; do not wait for a complete population count if a partial mailing can be made without materially misleading recipients.

B. 'In no case later than 60 calendar days'
- Hard ceiling. Absolute as to the count, subject only to § 164.412.
- Counting convention: the day of discovery is day 0. The deadline is the 60th calendar day after the date of discovery.
- Worked example 1: discovery on 3 March 2025. Day 0 = 3 Mar. Days 1–28 = 4–31 Mar. Days 29–58 = 1–30 Apr. Day 59 = 1 May. Day 60 = 2 May 2025. Deadline: 2 May 2025.
- Worked example 2: discovery on 1 February 2025. Day 0 = 1 Feb. Days 1–27 = 2–28 Feb. Days 28–58 = 1–31 Mar. Day 59 = 1 Apr. Day 60 = 2 Apr 2025. Deadline: 2 Apr 2025.
- No weekend/holiday rollover: if day 60 is a Saturday, the deadline is that Saturday, not the following Monday.
- The 60 days is per breach, not per individual; the deadline is the same for every individual in the same breach discovered on the same day.

C. 'After discovery of a breach'
- The clock is keyed to discovery, so the critical compliance artifact is a contemporaneous, defensible record of the discovery date.
- Imputed knowledge is the most common failure point. If a help-desk technician, a billing clerk, a security operations analyst, or an agent/vendor workforce member (other than the person who committed the breach) knew or should have known on day X, the covered entity is deemed to have discovered the breach on day X — even if in-house counsel was not told until day X+40.
- 'Reasonable diligence' means the entity is charged with what a diligent organization would have uncovered through ordinary monitoring, log review, and escalation channels. A breach sitting unread in a security queue is discovered when it landed in the queue, not when someone opened it.
- The date of the breach itself is relevant only to the content of the notice (§ 164.404(c)(1)(A) requires the date of breach and the date of discovery, if known); it does not start the clock.

=====================================================================
IV. QUALIFICATIONS THAT DO NOT CHANGE THE THREE ANSWERS
=====================================================================

1. § 164.412 — law-enforcement delay. The opening words of § 164.404(b) ('Except as provided in § 164.412') are the only textual carve-out. Where a law enforcement official states that notification would impede a criminal investigation or cause damage to national security, the covered entity delays as the official specifies in writing, or — if the statement is oral, or written without a specified period — for no more than 30 days from the date of the statement, documenting the statement and the official's identity, unless the oral statement is reduced to writing within that 30-day window. Once the impediment lifts, notification must go out without unreasonable delay. This suspends the 60-day clock; it does not reset it.

2. State law may be shorter. HIPAA sets a floor. A stricter state breach-notification statute (several impose 30 days, or 'most expedient time possible') is not preempted where it is more stringent (45 CFR § 160.203(b)). The operative deadline for any given breach is the earliest date required by any applicable law. Confirm the law of each affected individual's residence.

3. Business associates. § 164.404 binds covered entities. A business associate's duty runs to the covered entity under § 164.410 — notify the covered entity of the breach without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery. Because a business associate is typically an agent, its knowledge is generally imputed to the covered entity under § 164.404(a)(2), so the covered entity's own 60-day clock can start before the business associate's formal notice arrives. Do not treat the § 164.410 notice as the trigger by default.

4. Notification must still conform. Meeting the deadline is necessary but not sufficient. The notice must contain the § 164.404(c) elements and be delivered by a § 164.404(d) method (first-class mail to the last known address; email only if the individual agreed to electronic notice). Where contact information is insufficient or out of date for fewer than 10 individuals, alternative written, telephone, or oral notice is permitted; for 10 or more, substitute notice is required — conspicuous website posting for 90 days or conspicuous major-media notice, plus a toll-free number active at least 90 days.

=====================================================================
V. OPERATING PROCEDURE — FIXING THE DEADLINE ON A LIVE INCIDENT
=====================================================================

Step 1. Open a discovery log on the day the first credible indicator lands. Record date, time, source, and the role of the person who received it. Treat that date as day 0 unless a documented reasonable-diligence analysis pushes it earlier.

Step 2. Test imputation immediately. Ask who across the workforce and every agent/vendor knew or should have known, and when. If any such person knew earlier, reset day 0 to that earlier date. Record the conclusion and its basis.

Step 3. Compute the ceiling: day 0 + 60 calendar days. Write the resulting calendar date into the incident file. Do not compute in business days.

Step 4. Set internal milestones well inside the ceiling — target mailing by day 30–45 so that print, address verification, and call-center staging do not consume the statutory margin.

Step 5. Check for a shorter applicable state deadline for each affected individual's jurisdiction, and for any § 164.412 law-enforcement instruction. If § 164.412 applies, document the official's identity, the date, whether the statement was oral or written, and the period specified; calendar the resumption date.

Step 6. Prepare the § 164.404(c) content in parallel with the investigation; do not serialize.

Step 7. Send by a § 164.404(d) method and retain proof of mailing (date, address source, batch records).

Step 8. Document the entire timeline — discovery date and basis, imputation analysis, deadline computation, state-law analysis, any § 164.412 delay, and the send date — and retain it for six years. Under § 164.414(b) the covered entity bears the burden of demonstrating that notification was made as required, which in practice means proving the discovery date and the send date.

=====================================================================
VI. ASSUMPTIONS
=====================================================================

- The question is governed by the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule, 45 CFR §§ 164.400–414, and no narrower contractual or sector-specific regime displaces it.
- The entity is acting as a covered entity, not solely as a business associate; the § 164.410 duty is noted above but is not the answer given.
- No § 164.412 law-enforcement instruction and no shorter state statute is assumed; where either exists, the effective deadline is earlier or suspended as described in Part IV.
- The answers are read from the regulatory text as published at eCFR and GovInfo (current as of the fetch date), not from any organization-specific breach-response policy.

# MEMORANDUM — Regulation Z Right of Rescission: Deadline to Exercise, and Expiration Where the Notice or Material Disclosures Are Never Delivered

**Re:** 12 CFR § 1026.23(a)(3)(i)

**Authority relied on:** The text of § 1026.23 and the Official Interpretation of Paragraph 23(a)(3) (Comment 23(a)(3)-1) and of Paragraph 23(b)(1) (Comment 23(b)(1)-4), as published by the eCFR (12 CFR 1026.23), the CFPB (Regulation Z, § 1026.23) and the Federal Reserve Board, all retrieved 2026-11-23. Anything not found in those sources is marked **[VERIFY]** rather than asserted as sourced.

---

## 1. Constraint and questions presented

Ask 1 constrains the answer to a single clause: § 1026.23(a)(3)(i). That clause contains **both** rules asked about, and both figures below — 3 business days and 3 years — are the clause’s own numbers. Nothing is imported from TILA § 125 generally, from state law, or from practice.

- **Ask 2 (value):** until when may a consumer exercise the right to rescind a covered credit transaction?
- **Ask 3 (value):** when does the right expire if the required notice or material disclosures are never delivered?

---

## 2. Controlling text — § 1026.23(a)(3)

Clause (i), verbatim as retrieved:

> “The consumer may exercise the right to rescind until midnight of the third business day following consummation, delivery of the notice required by paragraph (b) of this section, or delivery of all material disclosures, whichever occurs last. If the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first. In the case of certain administrative proceedings, the rescission period shall be extended in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act.”

Clause (ii), verbatim:

> “For purposes of this paragraph (a)(3), the term ‘material disclosures’ means the required disclosures of the annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g).”

Clause (4) of the same paragraph: “When more than one consumer in a transaction has the right to rescind, the exercise of the right by one consumer shall be effective as to all consumers.”

---

## 3. Answer to Ask 2 — the ordinary deadline is midnight of the third business day after the last triggering event

**Answer: 3 business days.** The consumer may exercise the right until **midnight of the third business day following the last of three events**:

1. consummation of the transaction;
2. delivery of the notice required by § 1026.23(b);
3. delivery of all material disclosures as defined in § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii).

### Mechanics

- **(a) Whichever occurs last starts the clock.** Comment 23(a)(3)-1.i states the period “runs for 3 business days from the last of 3 events: A. Consummation of the transaction. B. Delivery of all material disclosures. C. Delivery to the consumer of the required rescission notice.”
- **(b) Counting.** The day of the triggering event is not counted; counting begins the next day, and only business days count (see § 5 below on what a business day is for rescission).
- **(c) How the right is exercised.** The consumer must “place the rescission notice in the mail, file it for telegraphic transmission, or deliver it to the creditor’s place of business within that period” (Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.B). Actual receipt by the creditor within the period is therefore not required if the consumer mails, files, or delivers within it.
- **(d) A late notice resets the clock.** The § 1026.23(b) notice need not precede consummation; if it is delivered afterwards, “the rescission period will not begin to run until the notice is given” (Comment 23(b)(1)-4: notice on May 15 with consummation and disclosures on May 10 → the 3-business-day period runs from May 15).
- **(e) One consumer’s exercise binds all.** § 1026.23(a)(4).
- **(f) No performance before expiry.** No money may be disbursed other than in escrow, no services performed, and no materials delivered until the rescission period has expired and the creditor is reasonably satisfied the consumer has not rescinded — § 1026.23(c).

### Worked computations

| Facts | Computation | Deadline |
|---|---|---|
| Consummated Fri June 1; disclosures and notice delivered Thu May 31 (Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.A) | Clock starts at the last event (June 1). Sat June 2 = day 1; Sun June 3 excluded; Mon June 4 = day 2; Tue June 5 = day 3 | **Midnight Tue June 5** |
| Disclosures and consummation Fri June 1; rescission notice delivered Mon June 4 (Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.B) | Clock starts June 4. Tue June 5 = 1; Wed June 6 = 2; Thu June 7 = 3 | **Midnight Thu June 7** |
| All three events Wed July 3, 2024 | Thu July 4 is Independence Day (excluded); Fri July 5 = 1; Sat July 6 = 2; Sun July 7 excluded; Mon July 8 = 3 | **Midnight Mon July 8, 2024** |

**Important boundary:** if the rescission notice or any material disclosure is **never** delivered, the second or third triggering event never occurs, the 3-business-day clock never starts, and Section 4 governs instead. The 3-business-day figure is therefore not the outer limit in a non-delivery case.

---

## 4. Answer to Ask 3 — where the notice or material disclosures are never delivered, the right expires at the earliest of three events, with 3 years as the ceiling

**Answer: 3 years after consummation — and earlier on either of two other events.** The clause provides that if “the required notice or material disclosures are not delivered, the right to rescind shall expire 3 years after consummation, upon transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property, or upon sale of the property, whichever occurs first.”

The right therefore expires at the **earliest** of:

1. **3 years after consummation** (the third anniversary of the consummation date);
2. **transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property**;
3. **sale of the property**.

### Points that matter in practice

- **The 3-year period is an outer limit, not a floor.** The right is never perpetual; the regulation does not leave a creditor exposed indefinitely because a notice was never sent.
- **The period runs from consummation**, not from discovery of the omission, not from a demand, and not from the consumer’s first awareness of the defect.
- **Either of the other two events ends the right before the third anniversary.** The practical answer to “when does it expire” is “whichever of the three happens first,” with 3 years as the maximum.
- **The clause is disjunctive.** Non-delivery of the § 1026.23(b) notice *or* of the material disclosures (any item listed in (a)(3)(ii)) produces the same extended expiration.
- **[VERIFY] Delivered-but-inaccurate disclosures.** The retrieved text states the trigger as non-delivery. Whether disclosures that were delivered but are inaccurate outside the § 1026.23(g)/(h) tolerances are treated as “not delivered” for this purpose is a point the commentary and case law have addressed; only the heading of § 1026.23(g)(1) (“One-half of 1 percent tolerance”) appears in the retrieved text. Confirm the full text of (g) and (h) and the official interpretation before relying on the extended period in an accuracy case.
- **[VERIFY] Foreclosure sales.** The regulatory words “upon sale of the property” are unqualified, but whether a foreclosure sale is such a sale is litigated; check the law of the relevant circuit before treating a foreclosure as terminating the right.
- **Administrative proceedings.** The clause’s final sentence extends the rescission period “in accordance with section 125(f) of the Act” (TILA § 125(f), 15 U.S.C. § 1635(f)) [VERIFY statutory text]. That is a **separate, proceeding-triggered** extension — it requires an enforcing agency to sue within 3 years and obtain a finding of violation — and is not an alternative general ceiling. Absent such a proceeding, the outer limit remains 3 years.

---

## 5. Definitions that drive both answers

**Material disclosures — § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii).** The annual percentage rate, the finance charge, the amount financed, the total of payments, the payment schedule, and the disclosures and limitations referred to in §§ 1026.32(c) and (d) and 1026.43(g). Omission of any one of these items, or of the § 1026.23(b) notice, moves the file into the extended period in Section 4.

**Notice — § 1026.23(b).** Two copies of the notice of the right to rescind to each consumer entitled to rescind (one copy if delivered electronically in accordance with E-Sign), on a separate document identifying the transaction, clearly and conspicuously disclosing: the retention or acquisition of a security interest in the principal dwelling; the consumer’s right to rescind; how to exercise it, with a form designating the creditor’s place of business; the effects of rescission under paragraph (d); and the date the rescission period expires. The Appendix H model form or a substantially similar notice satisfies § 1026.23(b)(2).

**Business day. [VERIFY]** For rescission purposes, “business day” means all calendar days except Sundays and the legal public holidays listed in 5 U.S.C. § 6103(a) (New Year’s Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Washington’s Birthday, Memorial Day, Independence Day, Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day). § 1026.2(a)(6) is not among the retrieved passages, but Comment 23(a)(3)-1.ii.A corroborates it: in that example Saturday June 2 is counted as one of the three days, which is only possible under the rescission-specific definition.

---

## 6. Scope — what counts as a covered credit transaction

§ 1026.23 applies to consumer credit transactions in which a security interest is or will be retained or acquired in the consumer’s principal dwelling, subject to the exemptions in § 1026.23(f). The retrieved text confirms the exemptions include: (1) a residential mortgage transaction; (2) a refinancing or consolidation by the same creditor of credit already secured by the principal dwelling, except to the extent the new amount financed exceeds the unpaid principal balance, earned unpaid finance charge, and costs of the refinancing; (3) a transaction in which a state agency is the creditor; (4) later advances in a series treated as a single transaction under § 1026.17(c)(6) where the notice and all material disclosures have been given; and (5) renewal of optional insurance premiums not treated as a refinancing under § 1026.20(a)(5). **[VERIFY]** the coverage language of § 1026.23(a)(1), which is not among the retrieved passages.

Scope matters because neither the 3-business-day rule nor the 3-year rule runs at all for an exempt transaction.

---

## 7. Compliance procedure (creditor / servicer / closing counsel)

1. **Fix and document the consummation date** from the note and closing documents.
2. **Determine coverage** under § 1026.23(a)(1) [VERIFY] and rule out each § 1026.23(f) exemption. If exempt, no rescission period runs.
3. **Confirm and evidence delivery** of (i) two copies of the § 1026.23(b) notice to each consumer entitled to rescind and (ii) every § 1026.23(a)(3)(ii) material disclosure. Retain proof of delivery, not merely proof of mailing.
4. **If all three triggering events are documented:** compute the deadline as **midnight of the third business day after the last of them**, counting calendar days except Sundays and the § 6103(a) holidays. Calendar that date before closing.
5. **Hold performance** — no disbursement other than in escrow, no services, no materials — until that deadline passes and the creditor is reasonably satisfied no rescission was sent (§ 1026.23(c)).
6. **If the notice or any material disclosure was never delivered:** do not close the file at day 3. Diary the **third anniversary of consummation**, and separately monitor for a transfer of all of the consumer’s interest or a sale of the property, either of which ends the right earlier.
7. **On a written rescission demand inside the open window:** treat it as timely if mailed, telegraphed, or delivered to the designated address within the period, and unwind under § 1026.23(d) (security interest void; no liability for amount financed or finance charge, subject to the tender provisions).
8. **If an enforcing agency sues within 3 years** and obtains a violation finding, re-diary the expiration under § 125(f) [VERIFY].

---

## 8. Bottom line

- **Ordinary case (Ask 2):** the consumer may rescind until **midnight of the third business day** following the last of consummation, delivery of the rescission notice, and delivery of all material disclosures — **3 business days**.
- **Non-delivery case (Ask 3):** the right expires at the earliest of **3 years after consummation**, transfer of all of the consumer’s interest in the property, or sale of the property — **3 years** is the outer limit, and the right is never perpetual.

Both figures come from the same clause, § 1026.23(a)(3)(i), as the constraint in Ask 1 requires.

Under 47 CFR § 97.313, the general maximum transmitter power for an amateur station is 1.5 kW PEP, and the lower limit that applies on the 10.10–10.15 MHz segment is 200 W PEP.

| Provision | Scope | Limit | Unit and measure |
|---|---|---:|---|
| 47 CFR § 97.313(b) | General amateur station ceiling | 1.5 kW PEP (1,500 W PEP) | kilowatts, peak envelope power |
| 47 CFR § 97.313(c)(1) | 10.10–10.15 MHz segment | 200 W PEP | watts, peak envelope power |

Governing text:

- § 97.313(b): “No station may transmit with a transmitter power exceeding 1.5 kW PEP.”
- § 97.313(c): “No station may transmit with a transmitter power output exceeding 200 W PEP: (1) On the 10.10-10.15 MHz segment;”

Measure: both figures are expressed in peak envelope power (PEP), the Part 97 measure of transmitter power, not effective radiated power (ERP) or equivalent isotropically radiated power (EIRP). The 200 W PEP figure in § 97.313(c)(1) is an absolute transmitter-power-output cap for that segment and is not adjusted for antenna gain.

Relationship between the two figures: the 1.5 kW PEP limit in § 97.313(b) is the general ceiling; the 200 W PEP limit in § 97.313(c)(1) is a lower band-specific ceiling that controls on 10.10–10.15 MHz. A station operating in that segment therefore cannot rely on the 1.5 kW general ceiling.

Separate operating duty: § 97.313(a) also requires an amateur station to “use the minimum transmitter power necessary to carry out the desired communications.” That is a minimum-power operating obligation, not a numeric maximum, and it does not change the two numeric ceilings above.

Source check: the quoted § 97.313(b) and § 97.313(c)(1) text is identical in the current eCFR text of 47 CFR § 97.313 and the 2025 CFR compilation (CFR-2025-title47-vol5, § 97.313). Other paragraphs of § 97.313 contain additional band-, mode-, license-class-, and location-specific limits, but they are outside this request.

question: P6
answer:
ANNUAL OCCUPATIONAL DOSE LIMITS FOR AN ADULT UNDER 10 CFR § 20.1201(a)

1. ANSWER TABLE

| # | Dose quantity (regulatory term) | Annual limit | Annual limit | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | Total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) | 5 rems | 0.05 Sv | § 20.1201(a)(1)(i) |
| 3 | Lens dose equivalent (lens of the eye) | 15 rems | 0.15 Sv | § 20.1201(a)(2)(i) |
| 4 | Shallow-dose equivalent, skin of the whole body | 50 rems | 0.5 Sv | § 20.1201(a)(2)(ii) |

Governing provision (ask 1): 10 CFR § 20.1201, 'Occupational dose limits for adults,' paragraph (a). Source text as currently published on eCFR (fetched 2026-11-23) and in the GovInfo 2026 and 2024 editions of 10 CFR Part 20; all renderings are identical for the three values above.

2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (§ 20.1201(a), in relevant part)

'(a) The licensee shall control the occupational dose to individual adults, except for planned special exposures under § 20.1206, to the following dose limits.
 (1) An annual limit, which is the more limiting of—
  (i) The total effective dose equivalent being equal to 5 rems (0.05 Sv); or
  (ii) The sum of the deep-dose equivalent and the committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens of the eye being equal to 50 rems (0.5 Sv).
 (2) The annual limits to the lens of the eye, to the skin of the whole body, and to the skin of the extremities, which are:
  (i) A lens dose equivalent of 15 rems (0.15 Sv), and
  (ii) A shallow-dose equivalent of 50 rem (0.5 Sv) to the skin of the whole body or to the skin of any extremity.'

3. UNIT CONVERSION (ask 5)

Basis: 1 Sv = 100 rem (1 rem = 0.01 Sv). All three conversions are exact; no rounding is applied.

- 5 rems / 100 = 0.05 Sv
- 15 rems / 100 = 0.15 Sv
- 50 rems / 100 = 0.5 Sv

These agree exactly with the sievert parentheticals printed in the regulation itself, which is an independent check on the arithmetic.

4. HEALTH-PHYSICS INTERPRETATION NOTES (needed to apply the numbers correctly)

(a) The 5-rem TEDE figure is not a free-standing number. § 20.1201(a)(1) sets 'an annual limit, which is the more limiting of' (i) TEDE = 5 rems, OR (ii) deep-dose equivalent + committed dose equivalent to any individual organ or tissue other than the lens = 50 rems (0.5 Sv). Compliance is demonstrated against whichever arm binds; in routine external-exposure monitoring the deep-dose equivalent is substituted for the effective dose equivalent under § 20.1201(c) unless an NRC-approved dosimetry method is used.

(b) The 50-rem organ figure in (a)(1)(ii) is NOT a whole-body limit and must not be reported as the skin or whole-body limit. The skin limit is the separate 50 rem shallow-dose equivalent in (a)(2)(ii). The two 50-rem values are numerically coincident but legally distinct.

(c) The lens, skin and extremity limits are excluded from the summation used to demonstrate TEDE compliance (Appendix B to Part 20, footnote to § 20.1202: 'The dose equivalents for the lens of the eye, the skin, and the extremities are not included in the summation, but are subject to separate limits.').

(d) 'Skin of the whole body' is limited by the shallow-dose equivalent, defined at a tissue depth of 0.007 cm (7 mg/cm²), and per § 20.1201(c) the assigned shallow-dose equivalent is averaged over the contiguous 10 cm² of skin receiving the highest exposure. The same 50-rem shallow-dose equivalent applies to the skin of any extremity (§ 20.1201(a)(2)(ii)) — the extremity limit was not requested and is listed here only to prevent conflation.

(e) Lens dose equivalent is defined at a tissue depth of 0.3 cm; deep-dose equivalent at 1 cm (10 mm) (§ 20.1003 definitions).

(f) All three are annual limits, per § 20.1201(a)(1) ('An annual limit') and (a)(2) ('The annual limits').

(g) Related limits that are NOT part of this answer and must not be substituted for it: minors = 10% of the adult limits (§ 20.1207); embryo/fetus of a declared pregnant woman = 0.5 rem (5 mSv) over the entire pregnancy (§ 20.1208(a)); planned special exposures (§ 20.1206) are excluded from the (a) control regime but are counted against lifetime limits; dose received in the current year while employed by another person must be subtracted (§ 20.1201(f), § 20.2104(e)).

5. VERIFICATION PERFORMED

- Cross-source agreement: identical figures in eCFR § 20.1201 (current), eCFR Part 20 landing page, GovInfo CFR-2026-title10-vol1 Part 20 Subpart C, and GovInfo CFR-2024-title10-vol1 § 20.1201 XML. No version conflict.
- Unit arithmetic: each rem value ÷ 100 equals the stated sievert value; the results match the regulation's own printed parentheticals.
- Internal consistency: lens (15 rem) < skin (50 rem); TEDE (5 rem) is the controlling whole-body value with the 50-rem organ arm as the alternative 'more limiting of' test; no stated value contradicts another threshold stated in this deliverable.
- Currency caveat (does not change the answer): the text carries amendment history through 72 FR 68059 (Dec. 4, 2007) and the current eCFR text still reads 15 rems (0.15 Sv) for the lens. The NRC has not, in the published text relied on here, replaced this with the ICRP-2011 recommendation of 20 mSv/yr averaged (50 mSv in any single year); if a future Part 20 amendment does so, the lens value here would be superseded. Verify against the then-current eCFR before using this in a licensing or compliance document.

## Answer — 49 CFR § 173.120(a)

**Threshold:** a Class 3 flammable liquid is a liquid having a flash point of **not more than 60 °C (140 °F)** — equivalently, **at or below 60 °C (140 °F)**.

| Unit | Flash point | Regulatory comparison |
|---|---|---|
| °C | 60 °C | not more than (≤) |
| °F | 140 °F | not more than (≤) |

These are one threshold, not two: 60 °C × 9/5 + 32 = 140 °F exactly.

### Regulatory text
> “For the purpose of this subchapter, a flammable liquid (Class 3) means a liquid having a flash point of not more than 60 °C (140 °F), or any material in a liquid phase with a flash point at or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) that is intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging, with the following exceptions: …”
> — 49 CFR § 173.120(a)

### How the comparison works
- **Exactly 60 °C (140 °F):** Class 3. The rule is “not more than,” so the boundary is inclusive.
- **Above 60 °C (140 °F):** not Class 3 on the flash-point limb. Under § 173.120(b)(1), a liquid with a flash point above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F) may be a combustible liquid if it meets no other hazard class.
- **At or above 37.8 °C (100 °F) and intentionally heated:** a material in a liquid phase intentionally heated and offered for transportation or transported at or above its flash point in a bulk packaging is Class 3 even if its flash point is above 60 °C. This is a separate route into Class 3; it does not move the 60 °C/140 °F flash-point threshold.

### Measurement basis
§ 173.120(c) specifies closed-cup flash-point test procedures (e.g., ASTM D 56, D 3278, D 3828 for certain low-viscosity single-phase liquids; ASTM D 93, D 3278, ISO 1516, ISO 1523 and others for other liquids). Apply the 60 °C/140 °F threshold to the closed-cup result; do not substitute open-cup results.

### Adjacent boundaries / exceptions (do not conflate)
- **Combustible liquid, § 173.120(b)(1):** flash point **above 60 °C (140 °F) and below 93 °C (200 °F)**. The 93 °C (200 °F) parenthetical is the regulation’s printed equivalent (93 °C ≈ 199.4 °F).
- **§ 173.120(a)(1)–(5)** carve out liquids that would otherwise fall at or below the threshold: liquids meeting § 173.115 definitions; mixtures with ≥99% by volume of components having a flash point of 60 °C (140 °F) or higher when not transported at or above the flash point; liquids with flash point >35 °C (95 °F) that do not sustain combustion (ASTM D 4206 or appendix H); liquids with flash point >35 °C (95 °F) and fire point >100 °C (212 °F) (ISO 2592); and liquids with flash point >35 °C (95 °F) in water-miscible solution with >90% water by mass.

### Note on 60.5 °C / 141 °F
The codified § 173.120(a) figure is **60 °C (140 °F)**. A 60.5 °C (141 °F) figure is not the § 173.120(a) threshold and should not be used for this classification.

question: P8
answer:
FALL PROTECTION TRIGGER AND PERMITTED SYSTEMS — 29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1)
(Safety Engineer's restatement of the regulatory text; a statement of what the standard requires, not legal advice. State-plan jurisdictions may adopt different or additional requirements and must be checked separately for the project location.)

1. ANSWER AS A COMPLIANCE STATEMENT

Ask 2 — Trigger height. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal or vertical) with an unprotected side or edge that is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level must be protected from falling. The threshold is 6 feet (1.8 m); below 6 feet, (b)(1) does not require fall protection (other paragraphs and other subparts may still apply).

Ask 3 — Permitted systems. Protection must be provided by the use of: (a) guardrail systems, (b) safety net systems, or (c) personal fall arrest systems. Those three are the only systems enumerated in (b)(1).

Combined one-line citation suitable for a compliance document, training slide, or specification:
"29 CFR § 1926.501(b)(1): each employee on a walking/working surface with an unprotected side or edge 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."

2. VERBATIM REGULATORY TEXT (as fetched; identical across sources)

"(b)(1) Unprotected sides and edges. Each employee on a walking/working surface (horizontal and vertical surface) with an unprotected side or edge which is 6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level shall be protected from falling by the use of guardrail systems, safety net systems, or personal fall arrest systems."
— https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/section-1926.501 (fetched 2026-11-23T12:38:17Z, sha256 3e4c6b147793)
— https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2025-title29-vol8/xml/CFR-2025-title29-vol8-sec1926-501.xml (fetched 2026-11-23T12:38:16Z, sha256 4b2282f0f73f)
— https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/chapter-XVII/part-1926/subpart-M (fetched 2026-11-23T12:38:17Z, sha256 84bf289259de)

Two independent official sources (eCFR current and the 2025 annual CFR edition on GovInfo) carry the same wording, so the 6-foot threshold and the three-system list are not an artifact of a single rendering.

3. HOW THE TERMS IN (b)(1) ARE BOUNDED (§ 1926.500 definitions, quoted)

- Walking/working surface: "any surface, whether horizontal or vertical on which an employee walks or works, including, but not limited to, floors, roofs, ramps, bridges, runways, formwork and concrete reinforcing steel but not including ladders, vehicles, or trailers, on which employees must be located in order to perform their job duties."
- Unprotected sides and edges: "any side or edge (except at entrances to points of access) of a walking/working surface, e.g., floor, roof, ramp, or runway where there is no wall or guardrail system at least 39 inches (1.0 m) high." Consequence for field use: an edge already closed by a wall or a guardrail at least 39 inches (1.0 m) high is not an "unprotected side or edge," so the (b)(1) trigger is not reached at that edge; the 39-inch figure is a definitional geometry test, not a fall-height threshold, and is independent of the 6-foot trigger.
- Guardrail system: "a barrier erected to prevent employees from falling to lower levels."
- Leading edge (relevant because a leading edge is treated as an unprotected side and edge when not under active construction): "the edge of a floor, roof, or formwork ... which changes location as additional floor, roof, decking, or formwork sections are placed, formed, or constructed. A leading edge is considered to be an 'unprotected side and edge' during periods when it is not actively and continuously under construction."
- Personal fall arrest system components are defined in the same section (body belt/safety belt, body harness, buckle, connector, lanyard), and "infeasible" is defined as impossible to perform the work using a conventional fall protection system (guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest) or technologically impossible to use any one of them.
- Design and performance criteria for each of the three systems (guardrail geometry and strength, safety net installation and strength, personal fall arrest anchorage, lifeline, deceleration and rescue) are in 29 CFR § 1926.502, not in (b)(1). This summary deliberately states no numeric criteria from § 1926.502, because that section's text was not among the fetched passages; the controlling numbers must be read from § 1926.502 directly when writing a specification.

4. SCOPE NOTES A SAFETY ENGINEER SHOULD CARRY FORWARD WITH THIS ANSWER

- (b)(1) is the general rule. Adjacent paragraphs in the same section cover specific exposures, several at the same 6-foot (1.8 m) trigger but with different permitted-system lists, e.g.: (b)(2) leading edges (guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest, with an infeasibility exception allowing a § 1926.502(k) fall protection plan); (b)(4) holes (personal fall arrest, covers, or guardrails around the hole); (b)(5) formwork and reinforcing steel (personal fall arrest, safety net, or positioning device systems); (b)(6) ramps, runways, and other walkways (guardrail systems); (b)(7)(ii) excavations (guardrails, fences, barricades, or covers); (b)(8) dangerous equipment (guardrail or equipment guards below 6 feet; guardrail, personal fall arrest, or safety net at 6 feet or more); (b)(9) overhand bricklaying (guardrail, safety net, personal fall arrest, or controlled access zone); (b)(14) wall openings; (b)(15) walking/working surfaces not otherwise addressed (guardrail, safety net, or personal fall arrest). Where a condition matches a specific paragraph, that paragraph's system list governs rather than (b)(1)'s.
- Exclusions from subpart M coverage are set by § 1926.500(a)(2); (b)(15) is expressly subject to both § 1926.500(a)(2) and (b)(1)–(b)(14). Confirm applicability before applying (b)(1).
- (b)(1) contains no infeasibility exception on its face (unlike (b)(2)(i)); do not import the leading-edge fall-protection-plan exception into (b)(1) without a documented basis.
- This is the construction standard (29 CFR part 1926). General-industry fall protection (29 CFR part 1910 subpart D) uses a different trigger and is outside this answer.

5. RECORD OF THE TWO PROOFS OF ABSENCE AND WHY THEY DO NOT SUPPRESS ASKS 2 AND 3

- Ask 2 proof: none of '6 feet', '1.8 m', '6 feet (1.8 m)', '6 feet (1.8 m) or more', '6 feet (1.8 m) or more above a lower level' appears in the full text of https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1926/subpart-M/section-1926.500 (13,390 characters; sha256 909e30967f5d). That page is the definitions section; it defines terms and states no fall-protection trigger. It is not the page the ask is about.
- Ask 3 proof: none of 'guardrail systems', 'safety net systems', 'personal fall arrest systems' appears in the full text of https://ecfr.gov/current/title-29/part-1926/subpart-D (563,034 characters; sha256 ef4f711c2a24). Subpart D covers occupational health and environmental controls (the fetched passages are lead and hazardous-waste-operations training text). It is not the page the ask is about.
- Disposition: both proofs establish silence on pages other than § 1926.501. The cited provision itself is present verbatim in three fetched renderings (Section 2 above) and states both the 6-foot (1.8 m) trigger and the three permitted systems. Because the answer to asks 2 and 3 is not 'the page states none' but is printed in the governing section, neither ask is listed in not_stated, and neither is blocked. No figure is withheld.

6. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR THE REVIEWER

- Trigger quoted at 6 feet (1.8 m) — matches eCFR, GovInfo 2025 CFR, and the subpart-M page. No competing height value is stated anywhere in this deliverable.
- Systems quoted as exactly three — guardrail systems, safety net systems, personal fall arrest systems — no fourth system added and none dropped.
- 39 inches (1.0 m) appears only as the § 1926.500 definitional wall/guardrail height, which is below the 6-foot trigger and therefore cannot contradict it.
- No numeric criteria from § 1926.502 are asserted; that section is cited only as the location of the system design requirements.
- Citation form, source URLs, fetch timestamps, and SHA-256 digests are supplied above so the text can be re-verified against the current eCFR before use in a controlled compliance document.

question: P9
answer:
RFC 1918 ("Address Allocation for Private Internets", BCP 5, February 1996), Section 3, reserves exactly three blocks of IPv4 unicast address space for private internets. The answer below is quoted-and-derived from that section; nothing here depends on later allocations or amendments.

THE THREE BLOCKS

| # | RFC 1918 name | Address range | CIDR prefix | Dotted-quad mask | Host bits | Addresses |
|---|---------------|---------------|-------------|------------------|-----------|-----------|
| 1 | "24-bit block" | 10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 | 10.0.0.0/8 (10/8) | 255.0.0.0 | 24 | 16,777,216 |
| 2 | "20-bit block" | 172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 | 172.16.0.0/12 (172.16/12) | 255.240.0.0 | 20 | 1,048,576 |
| 3 | "16-bit block" | 192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 | 192.168.0.0/16 (192.168/16) | 255.255.0.0 | 16 | 65,536 |

Total reserved: 17,891,328 addresses, i.e. 2^24 + 2^20 + 2^16 = 1/256 + 1/4096 + 1/65536 of the 2^32 space = 0.4166% (about 0.417%).

RFC 1918's own wording of the three entries, verbatim:

    10.0.0.0        -   10.255.255.255  (10/8 prefix)
    172.16.0.0      -   172.31.255.255  (172.16/12 prefix)
    192.168.0.0     -   192.168.255.255 (192.168/16 prefix)

HOW EACH RANGE FOLLOWS FROM ITS PREFIX (derivation, not memory)

1. /8 fixes 8 leading bits, i.e. the first octet only (10). The remaining 24 bits are free: 10.0.0.0 through 10.255.255.255. This is one former class A network number.
2. /12 fixes 12 leading bits: the whole first octet (172) plus the high 4 bits of the second octet. The high nibble is 0001, so the second octet ranges over 00010000-00011111 = 16-31. Third and fourth octets are entirely free: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255. This is 16 contiguous former class B network numbers (172.16 through 172.31).
3. /16 fixes 16 leading bits: the first two octets (192.168). Third and fourth octets free: 192.168.0.0 through 192.168.255.255. This is 256 contiguous former class C network numbers.

The RFC's names "24-bit", "20-bit" and "16-bit" block refer to the number of host bits left free, which is why the 24-bit block is the largest and the 16-bit block the smallest.

NOTATION AND COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID

- 172.16.0.0/12 is 172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255, NOT 172.16.0.0-172.16.255.255. The latter would be 172.16.0.0/16 and is the single most frequent misstatement of RFC 1918. The second octet must be allowed to run to 31.
- All three prefixes are written with host bits zero in the network address (10.0.0.0, 172.16.0.0, 192.168.0.0). Writing 10.0.0.0/8 as "10/8" is acceptable shorthand and is what RFC 1918 itself uses in parentheses; the full form is preferred in configuration.
- These three blocks are the only RFC 1918 private ranges. The following are special-purpose but are NOT RFC 1918 private space and must not be substituted for it: 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598 shared address space / carrier-grade NAT), 169.254.0.0/16 (RFC 3927 link-local), 127.0.0.0/8 (loopback), 0.0.0.0/8, 240.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255/32.

CITATION NOTE (correction to a stated assumption)

The project analysis assumed "RFC 1918 as originally published (1994)". RFC 1918 is dated February 1996 and is BCP 5; the 1994 document carrying these same three blocks is RFC 1597 (March 1994), which RFC 1918 obsoleted. The three blocks and their prefixes are identical in both documents, so the answer is unchanged; the correct citation for the current specification is RFC 1918 (February 1996). No later RFC has added or removed an RFC 1918 private block (RFC 6319, July 2011, examined the question of adding more private IPv4 space and did not recommend doing so), so the answer is stable and the citation date is the only thing that needed fixing.

OPERATIONAL MEANING (one line, since the ask is factual)

These blocks may be used by any enterprise without coordination with IANA or an Internet registry, are unique only within the using network(s), and packets sourced from them must not appear on the public Internet (RFC 1918 §3-§5; RIPE NCC restates the same three blocks).

question: P10
answer:
LEGAL ANSWER — Working Time Regulations 1998 (SI 1998/1833), regulation 4(1): the 48-hour average and the route out of it

1. THE LIMIT — 48 HOURS

Regulation 4(1) (text as originally made, and reproduced verbatim in the 'latest available (revised)' version supplied):

"Subject to regulation 5, a worker's working time, including overtime, in any reference period which is applicable in his case shall not exceed an average of 48 hours for each seven days."

In the amended text the opening words are replaced by: "Unless his employer has first obtained the worker's agreement in writing to perform such work, ...".

Answer to ask 1: the limit is an average of 48 hours for each seven days.

Four features of the limit matter and are routinely got wrong:

(a) It is an average, not a weekly ceiling. A worker may lawfully work more than 48 hours in a given week provided that, averaged across the applicable reference period, working time does not exceed 48 hours per seven days. Nothing in regulation 4 makes any single week a breach.

(b) Overtime counts. The words "including overtime" are express. A worker contracted for 40 hours can therefore average no more than 8 hours' overtime per week across the reference period before the limit is exceeded; there is no carve-out for voluntary, occasional or premium-paid overtime.

(c) The averaging window. Regulation 4(3): subject to paragraphs (4) and (5) and to any agreement under regulation 23(b), the reference period is (a) where a relevant agreement provides for successive periods of 17 weeks, each such period, or (b) otherwise, any period of 17 weeks in the course of employment. Regulation 4(4): where the worker has been employed for less than 17 weeks, the reference period is the period since he started work. Regulation 4(5): for a worker excluded from certain provisions by regulation 21, '17 weeks' is read as '26 weeks'. The 26-week figure changes the averaging window only — the 48-hour limit is unchanged.

(d) The averaging formula and excluded days. Regulation 4(6): average weekly working time = (A + B) / C, where A is aggregate working hours in the reference period, B is aggregate working hours in the period immediately after the reference period ending when the number of days worked equals the number of excluded days in the reference period, and C is the number of weeks in the reference period. Regulation 4(7) defines 'excluded days' as days in annual leave under regulation 13 (as amended, also 13A and 15B), sick leave, maternity (as amended, also paternity, adoption and parental) leave, and any period in respect of which the regulation 4(1) limit did not apply by reason of the worker's written agreement.

The employer's duty is in regulation 4(2): to take all reasonable steps, in keeping with the need to protect health and safety, to ensure the limit is complied with for each worker to whom it applies; and, as amended, to keep up-to-date records of all workers who carry out work to which the limit does not apply because the employer has obtained the worker's written agreement.

2. HOW A WORKER MAY BE TAKEN OUTSIDE THE LIMIT — THE INDIVIDUAL WRITTEN OPT-OUT (REGULATION 5(1))

Mechanism: the worker agrees with the employer in writing that the limit shall not apply in his case. Regulation 5(1):

"The limit specified in regulation 4(1) shall not apply in relation to a worker who has agreed with his employer in writing that it should not apply in his case, provided that the employer complies with the requirements of paragraph (4)."

Regulation 5(2) and (3) supply the terms of that agreement:

- Duration — regulation 5(2)(a): the agreement may relate to a specified period or apply indefinitely.
- Withdrawal by the worker — regulation 5(2)(b): subject to any provision in the agreement for a different period of notice, it is terminable by the worker by giving not less than seven days' notice to the employer in writing.
- Cap on agreed notice — regulation 5(3): where the agreement provides for termination after a period of notice, that notice period must not exceed three months.

The amended regulation 4(1) adds a timing condition: the employer must have "first obtained" the worker's written agreement to perform such work — i.e. the opt-out must be in place before the worker performs working time that would otherwise breach the 48-hour average, not ratified afterwards.

Conditions and consequences in practice:

1. Writing. The agreement must be in writing and must be an agreement that the regulation 4(1) limit is not to apply. A written contract term can serve, provided it is a genuine agreement to disapply the limit and not merely an acknowledgment that long hours may occur.

2. Timing. Obtain the agreement before the work exceeding the limit is performed (regulation 4(1) as amended, "first obtained").

3. Records. The employer must keep up-to-date records of every worker carrying out work to which the limit does not apply by reason of such an agreement (regulation 4(2) as amended), and must comply with regulation 5(4) (the paragraph is cross-referenced in regulation 5(1); see verification note V3 below before relying on its detail).

4. Withdrawal. The worker may terminate the agreement on not less than seven days' written notice, unless the agreement provides a different notice period, which cannot exceed three months. On termination the 48-hour average applies again from that point; the employer must then schedule within the limit.

5. Effect is narrow. The opt-out disapplies regulation 4(1) only. It does not disapply the night-work limits (regulation 6), the rest period and break entitlements (regulations 10-12), the 48-hour weekly rest entitlement (regulation 11), the annual leave entitlement, or the employer's health-and-safety duty under regulation 4(2) in respect of workers to whom the limit still applies.

6. Not a contractual entitlement to work long hours. The opt-out removes a regulatory ceiling; it does not oblige the employer to offer, or the worker to accept, overtime.

3. OTHER ROUTES THAT ARE DISTINCT FROM THE REGULATION 5 OPT-OUT (flagged for verification — see V4)

These exist but must not be conflated with the opt-out:

- Unmeasured working time (regulation 19): where, because of the specific characteristics of the work, the duration of working time is not measured or predetermined, or can be determined by the worker himself (the paradigm case being managing executives and similar autonomous workers), specified provisions — understood to include regulation 4(1) and (2) — do not apply. This is a category exclusion, not an agreement.
- Workforce and collective agreements (regulation 23): regulation 4(3) is expressly subject to "any agreement under regulation 23(b)", which can modify the reference periods. This changes the averaging window, not the 48-hour figure.
- Regulation 21 workers: a 26-week reference period is substituted (regulation 4(5)); the worker remains within regulation 4, with a longer window.
- Part III exceptions generally: regulation 3 provides that Part II has effect subject to the exceptions in Part III, which cover specified sectors and worker categories (including seagoing and fisheries work). Workers excluded from the Regulations entirely fall outside regulation 4 altogether — a different proposition from opting out.
- Young workers: separate limits apply to young workers, and the regulation 5 opt-out is not the route by which those limits are varied. Verify the applicable provision (understood to be regulation 5A) before advising in any case involving a worker under 18.

4. VERSION AND VERIFICATION NOTES

V1. The 48-hour figure and the regulation 5(1) mechanism are quoted verbatim from the supplied sources and are identical in the as-made, 1998-10-01, 2003-08-01 and latest-available versions. The answer to both asks does not depend on which version is used.

V2. Reference period. The text supplied, including the "latest available (revised)" page, states 17 weeks in regulation 4(3). That same page lists a 01/01/2024 amendment among the versions of section 4. Before advising on the averaging window for any period on or after 1 January 2024, check the current revised text of regulation 4(3) to confirm whether the reference period has been extended. This does not affect the 48-hour figure.

V3. Regulation 5(4). The supplied extract of regulation 5(1) cross-refers to "the requirements of paragraph (4)" but the text of paragraph (4) was not in the material available. Do not paraphrase it; read it from the current revised text before drafting or auditing an opt-out agreement. The record-keeping obligation in regulation 4(2) as amended is quoted and can be relied on as stated.

V4. Section 3 above is drawn from the structure of the Regulations and is marked accordingly: the regulation 19 list of disapplied provisions, the exact scope of regulation 23(b) agreements, the Part III exclusion categories, and the young-worker provision should each be confirmed against the current revised text before being relied on in advice. None of them is part of the answer to either ask; they are supplied only so that the opt-out is not mistaken for the only route out of regulation 4.

V5. This is a general statement of the law of England and Wales and Scotland (regulation 4 is marked E+W+S), not advice on any particular worker, contract or rota. Applying it requires the actual reference period, the actual hours including overtime, and the actual opt-out documentation.
